subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Present Bias and Hyperbolic Discounting
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Present Bias and Hyperbolic Discounting.

hook.text: Would you rather have $100 today or $110 tomorrow? Most pick today. $100 in 30 days vs $110 in 31? Most wait.

buildup.text: Present bias: we overvalue immediate rewards relative to future ones. The nearer the reward, the more it dominates.

discovery.text: Hyperbolic discounting means our discount rate isn't constant. We're patient about the distant future and impatient.

twist.text: This is why January gym memberships spike and February attendance drops. Future-self made a plan.

climax.text: Pre-commit when you're patient. Automate savings, schedule workouts, and remove the decision from your impatient.

punchline.text: Your patient future self needs protection from your impatient present self.

quiz.question: What does present bias cause?
options: Equal valuation of present and future rewards
Overvaluing immediate rewards relative to future ones
Preferring future rewards over present ones

details.summary: Present bias is the tendency to disproportionately prefer immediate rewards over future ones, even when waiting produces much greater value. Hyperbolic discounting means people discount the near future steeply but the far future almost flatly.
details.whyItMatters: Present bias is the primary obstacle to saving, investing, and healthy financial planning. People know they should save for retirement but the immediate pleasure of spending today overwhelms the abstract future benefit.
takeaways: Immediate rewards feel disproportionately more valuable than future ones
Discounting is steep for the near future but flat for the distant future
Present bias explains undersaving, overspending, and procrastination

faq.question: What is the difference between present bias and impatience?
faq.answer: Simple impatience would discount all future periods equally. Present bias specifically overweights the immediate present relative to any future period. Someone with present bias prefers $100 today over $110 tomorrow but is fine waiting from day 30 to day 31.

faq.question: How does present bias affect retirement saving?
faq.answer: The benefits of saving are decades away while the cost is immediate reduced spending. Present bias makes each paycheck's retirement contribution feel like a sacrifice for a distant stranger, your future self, who feels more abstract than real.
